lesson_title: Interest, Banking and Inflation: the Snowball and the Melting Note
hook_text: R100 under the mattress for ten years. Still says R100. Now worth R55. Nobody touched it.
clip_script: Your money is never standing still — it's either growing or melting. Gogo has R8 000 and two offers, both 7,5%. Simple interest pays R600 a year, every year, forever — it only ever looks at the original R8 000. A straight line. Compound interest is a snowball: year one, 8 000 becomes 8 600. Year two it grows the WHOLE 8 600 — R645. Year three, R693. After three years the snowball leads by R138. After twenty? Thousands. Same rate, same money — the only difference is what the interest is allowed to touch. Now the villain: inflation. Bread at R19,50 rides the same compound machine at 6% — R20,67, then R21,91. Your R100 note buys five loaves today, four in two years, and after ten years of 6% it keeps about R55 of its power. Cash under the mattress isn't safe — it's melting on schedule. So the rule: money must grow FASTER than prices climb, or it's shrinking in disguise. Earn above inflation, hunt your bank fees, and let the snowball roll.
visual_style: A split screen: a ruler-straight staircase of R600 steps against a snowball rolling and swelling down a hill; a bank statement with fee lines glowing red; a R100 note slowly shrinking beside a loaf of bread whose price tag ticks upward.
mood: Streetwise and protective, the voice of someone who checks the interest rate before signing anything.
pacing: Brisk through the two offers, a beat on each year of the snowball, then slow and deliberate as the note melts and the final rule lands.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and put your money on the winning side of the race.
